then.text: Best riding in years. You've ridden the marches with me, and the town will remember. Come back next June and bring a horse.

You've ridden all three marches and fought off a rival of the next town? Magnificent! I'll tell the town. The colours go back to the Provost on the day. Here's a sash of the Cornet's own, for services to the town.
Have you the colours from Ma Haig? The marches are at Scott's View, the Ford and the Eildon Gate. Ride them in that order. The rest is horses.

else.text: Och, you've arrived at last. I'm the Cornet this year, chosen by the town to carry the standard at the Common Riding. It's the greatest honour a young man in the Borders can have, and I've lost my colours.

We 'ride the marches': the old boundaries of the town's common land, to check that no neighbour has shifted a stone. It's an old custom, going back to the days of the reivers. Would you ride them for me? I'm needed here, with the horses.

then.text: Grand. Ma Haig at the bakehouse has the colours. Then the three marches: Scott's View, the Ford and the Eildon Gate. There's a steward at each. Watch for riders from the next town.

else.text: Och, well. The horses are in no hurry.

stable_lass.text: The Cornet gets all the glory, but it's the horses that do the work. Each rider polishes the tack for a week, plaits the mane and puts their best coat on. The horse just wants an apple.

At Hawick, the Common Riding celebrates the young men who captured an English flag at Hornshole in 1514, a year after Flodden. At Selkirk, they cast the colours in memory of the soldiers who didn't come home. It's a very serious fun day.
